competitors.name: Printable PDF caregiver log / shared Google Doc / spiral notebook on the counter
competitors.note: This is what families actually use. printblame.com ships 14 free caregiver daily-checklist PDFs; mysagebeam.com has a one-page daily care sheet, a home-caregiver shift report template and a weekly family summary; carehomecare.com publishes a '24-Hour Home Care Communication Log' PDF; familycaregiversonline.net gives a free activity log in PDF + Word; 101planners has a free medication log. Strengths: zero learning curve, works for an 80-year-old aide, is legally/emotionally 'real', and hands to a doctor instantly. Weaknesses: only exists in one physical place, illegible handwriting, the out-of-state sibling never sees it, no way to answer 'did anyone give the 2pm pill?' from the car. Our app must beat paper on remote visibility and double-dose safety while printing back out to something that looks like the paper they left behind.

competitors.name: CaringBridge
competitors.note: Category default; hospitals hand out the URL. Strong for broadcasting health updates to a wide circle of friends. Weak as an operational log: Keepsake's 2026 roundup says it 'feels dated', has unreliable notifications, and is 'designed for periodic updates, not daily logistics'. Users report it 'freezes up randomly', is 'behind in terms of current tech', and does not notify you when someone comments or replies. Its donation solicitation is the single most-resented thing about it (see complaints).

competitors.name: Lotsa Helping Hands
competitors.note: Best-known tool for delegating meals/rides via a volunteer sign-up calendar. Keepsake's roundup puts its app ratings in the 'mid-2s' with sync delays and an outdated UX that 'has not kept pace with newer competitors'. Reviewers report crashes during login/navigation, no ability to edit a note or announcement after posting, one-photo-at-a-time uploads, and no calendar or daily check-in place for medications. Task-scheduling scope, not a care log.

competitors.name: Caring Village
competitors.model: Free tier = 1 village, 2 members, WITH ADS. Circle $14.99/mo (2 villages, 5 members each). Village $24.99/mo (5 villages, 50 members each). 17% off annual.
competitors.note: Verified directly from caringvillage.com/pricing. The most aggressive paywall in the category and the most exploitable: 'Ad-free experience' is itself a paid feature, and document folders, printable care calendar, wellness-journal export and calendar integration are all gated. A free tier capped at 2 members is smaller than almost any real care team.

competitors.name: CircleOf
competitors.model: freemium — the person who creates the care circle pays the subscription
competitors.note: Task/care-team coordination. Keepsake flags the structural problem: the creator must commit to a subscription at exactly the moment care begins and nobody knows whether it will last three weeks or three years.

competitors.name: ianacare
competitors.model: free core app; premium tier sold to employers as a benefit
competitors.note: Well-regarded for mobilizing a support network around task requests. Weaknesses per Keepsake: no voice-memo capability, task-focused rather than journal-oriented, thin on appointment detail sharing, and it only works if you can actually get a support network to join.

competitors.name: Neela
competitors.note: Newer, polished all-in-one family caregiver app; iOS and web only, no Android. Publishes the category's most useful feature checklist (shared calendar, med management, document storage, role-based access, symptom tracking, cross-device sync) — useful as a table-stakes reference even though we can't match the server-side half.

competitors.name: Medisafe
competitors.model: free tier limited to 2 medications since Jan 2026; Premium $4.99/mo / $59.88/yr
competitors.note: Not a shared log, but it owns 'meds given' in users' heads, so we're compared to it. Its Jan-2026 move to subscription is the loudest grievance in the adjacent category: reports, family sharing and most reminder customization all went behind the paywall. Note our own portfolio already has pill-schedule — Caregiver Log should log doses *given* by a person, not build schedules.

complaints.complaint: CaringBridge's 'Tributes' link reads as donating to the family, but every dollar goes to CaringBridge. One user said the site made about $650 off her husband's cancer page — money she says could have gone to medical costs. Others described the wording as 'shady' and only learned by accident that they were funding the company, not the patient.
complaints.source: ComplaintsBoard caringbridge thread; corroborated in a TheSabre.com forum thread ('caring bridge will hit up the people you send a [link] to')
complaints.weWinIf: The tip jar never appears on the shared/read view that relatives open — only in Settings/About on the owner's device, worded unambiguously as supporting the app's developer, never 'support this family'. No suggested-amount modal, no interstitial, no ask on a page that a grieving person sent to forty people.

complaints.complaint: 'You can not edit any notes or announcements if you misspelled a word. You can not edit pictures or albums if you want to move or remove a picture and it only uploads one picture at a time.'
complaints.source: Lotsa Helping Hands negative app reviews (surfaced via AppGrooves/marlvel.ai sentiment summaries)
complaints.weWinIf: Every entry is editable and deletable forever, inline, in one tap — including after the link has been shared. Fixing a typo at 2am must not require deleting and re-typing the entry.

complaints.complaint: 'Frequent application crashes during login or navigation prevent access to essential community coordination features.' Users also report feature-parity gaps between the app and the website.
complaints.source: marlvel.ai 2026 sentiment report on Lotsa Helping Hands; Google Play / App Store reviews
complaints.weWinIf: There is no login to crash and no second platform to drift out of parity with. The app is one browser page; opening it is the login. Say this out loud on the landing screen.

complaints.complaint: Medisafe capped free users at 2 medications in Jan 2026. Long-time users: they 'had been using the app for years free while making lots of money from advertising, and now view the charging as just greed'. Commenters point out the average person with a chronic condition takes 4–5 daily meds, so the free tier is useless by design.
complaints.source: Trustpilot medisafe.com; pillo.care 'Medisafe Is Not Free Anymore' (2026); App Store reviews
complaints.weWinIf: No counters anywhere. Unlimited medications, entries, caregivers, days, share links. Critically: never render a locked/greyed feature — a disabled control with a lock icon is the visual grammar of the thing they're fleeing.

complaints.complaint: A free caregiving app for families in crisis carries third-party ads (Lotsa Helping Hands), while Caring Village sells 'Ad-free experience' as a $14.99/mo upgrade.
complaints.source: Keepsake 'honest 2026 guide to family caregiver apps'; caringvillage.com/pricing
complaints.weWinIf: Ad-free stated as a promise on the first screen and again on the shared read view, so the relative who opens the link sees a clean page and not a banner next to 'Mom had a hard night.'

complaints.complaint: 'The single biggest reason these apps fail is getting your family to actually use them. The friction is real — a tech-resistant parent, a sibling who won't download anything new, a cousin who prefers group text chaos. The best features in the world are useless if you're the only one using them.'
complaints.source: Keepsake 'honest 2026 guide to family caregiver apps' (2026); echoed by kinnect.club
complaints.weWinIf: This is our whole thesis. A read link opens in any browser with no install, no account, no email, no app store. The share flow's success metric is 'the 78-year-old aunt tapped the text message and saw the log' — design and test for exactly that path, including a QR code for handing the link to someone standing next to you.

complaints.complaint: 'If one sibling has an iPhone and another has a Pixel, you either pick a web-or-Android-and-iOS app or you accept that the iOS-only sibling is the captain.' Keepsake itself is iOS-only; Neela is iOS+web only.
complaints.source: Keepsake 'honest 2026 guide to family caregiver apps'
complaints.weWinIf: A browser PWA is inherently cross-platform. Make it explicit in the pitch — 'works on whatever phone your brother has' — because families have been burned and won't assume it.

complaints.complaint: Caring Village's free plan allows 2 members in 1 village. Real care teams are a primary caregiver, two or three siblings, a hired aide, and sometimes a neighbor — six-plus people.
complaints.weWinIf: Unlimited people on a link, and no concept of 'seats' in the UI at all. The word 'member' should not appear.

complaints.complaint: CaringBridge 'does not notify you when someone has posted a comment or when you have replied'; setup for email notifications 'may require a bit of trial and error'. Families end up running two systems — CaringBridge for the circle and a group text for 'did she get her 2pm pill'.
complaints.source: justuseapp CaringBridge review summary; ACAP Community platform review; Keepsake roundup
complaints.weWinIf: We cannot send push notifications, so we must not pretend to. Instead make the shared view self-evidently complete: a big 'last updated 22 min ago by Dana' header and a locally-computed 'new since you last looked' divider, so nobody has to ask whether they missed something. One timeline holds both the one-tap 'gave 2pm Donepezil' and the paragraph about confusion in the afternoon.

complaints.complaint: Senior-care and caregiver apps show 'a mixed landscape of privacy practices' — several 'made vague commitments about data security without outlining the safeguards in place'. Family caregiver apps are generally not HIPAA-covered entities, so the protections users assume exist mostly don't.
complaints.source: arXiv 2410.14607 'Evaluating Privacy Measures in Healthcare Apps Predominantly Used by Older Adults'; AARP health-information-privacy guidance; GiveCare privacy policy (explicitly 'non-HIPAA')
complaints.weWinIf: Make the literal, checkable claim: the log lives in this browser on this device and is never uploaded. One screen, plain language, no legalese. And be the only app in the category that is honest about link security — before generating a share link, state that the link is unlisted but not secret, anyone holding it can read the log, and offer revoke/regenerate.

complaints.complaint: App-store searches for 'caregiver app' are dominated by hiring marketplaces with subscription traps: users report signing up and getting 'stuck in a loop' unable to reach their account to cancel, a no-refund policy, and accounts removed 'without any further explanation'.
complaints.source: Care.com reviews on Trustpilot, BBB, ComplaintsBoard and the iOS App Store
complaints.weWinIf: Positioning must instantly read 'shared family notebook', not 'hire a caregiver'. No pricing page, no 'start free trial', no 'plans' link, no email capture — the absence of commercial furniture is itself the differentiator, and it should be visible within two seconds of landing.

complaints.complaint: Caregivers are told, across every guide, to arrive at appointments with a current med list, symptom notes and a 'mention at the next appointment' list — and the standing advice is still to keep a printed copy in a binder, a folded copy in a wallet, and a photo on the phone, because no app produces a doctor-ready page.
complaints.source: National Institute on Aging 'Taking Someone to a Doctor's Appointment'; caregiveraction.org Doctor Visit Checklist; SingleCare medication list templates
complaints.weWinIf: One button produces a clean one-page printable summary of the last N days plus the standing med list and the running 'ask the doctor' list. This is the moment the app proves it was worth using, and none of the free competitors do it well.

tableStakes: Timestamped entries that default to now but are trivially back-datable — the 6am entry gets written at 9am, and a wrong timestamp on a medication is worse than no entry.
Attribution on every entry: who logged it, set once per device with no account. A log with unattributed entries is useless the moment two people disagree about what happened.

Medication-given as a distinct one-tap action separate from free-text notes, capturing drug, dose and time, with a visible 'already given today' state. Preventing a double dose is the safety reason this category exists.
Reverse-chronological timeline grouped by day, with a 'Today' anchor and a way to jump to a date — every printable template in the category is organized by day and users expect that shape.
A read-only share link that renders the entire log in a browser with no install and no account.
Print / PDF export of a date range. The log's real destination is a doctor's hands; NIA and Caregiver Action both treat the appointment handoff as the core artifact.
Data that survives reload, tab close, and being offline — entries get typed in a hospital basement with no signal and must not evaporate.
Entries editable and deletable after the fact, including after sharing. Lotsa Helping Hands is actively hated for the absence of this.

A standing reference block that is not a log entry: current medications with doses, allergies, doctors and phone numbers, pharmacy, insurance, and where the advance directive / DNR lives. Every free printable in this category has this section.

File-based export and import (JSON or plain text) for backup and device migration. With no cloud account, we own the backup story, and a caregiver who loses a year of logs to a cleared browser will never forgive it.
differentiators: Zero-install read link as the hero feature, QR code included. This attacks the category's documented #1 failure mode — 'a sibling who won't download anything new' — head on, and it is the one thing every funded competitor structurally cannot do because their business model needs the account.

Double-dose guard: tapping to log a medication first shows, in large type, when that med was last given and by whom, and requires an explicit confirm if it falls inside the interval. No competitor makes this the hero interaction, and it is the failure everyone in a multi-caregiver household actually fears.

'Print the last 7 days for the doctor' — one button, one clean page: meds given, notable changes, and the questions list. Turns the log into the appointment artifact that the free PDFs and the paid apps both fail to produce.

A running 'ask at the next appointment' list that anyone can add to from inside a log entry and that prints at the top of the doctor summary. Directly lifted from what caregiving guides tell people to keep on paper.

A shift-handoff composer with the four fields every printable handoff template uses (meds, food/fluids, mood/behavior, for the next person) so an exhausted caregiver never faces a blank box. Blank-box paralysis is why paper logs go empty.

Browser-native dictation as a first-class entry path. Keepsake's roundup singles out ianacare and CaringBridge for lacking voice capture; we can't store audio, but we can make the mic the obvious way to write at 2am one-handed.

Honest link-security copy plus revoke/regenerate on the share screen: 'anyone with this link can read the log.' Nobody in this category tells the truth about unlisted links, and for a family that may include an estranged sibling, that honesty is the trust-builder.

Paper-parity starter structure: the log's default sections mirror the free printable caregiver PDFs people already use, so moving off the counter notebook is a translation rather than a re-learn — and the printout looks like the thing they left behind.

aesthetic.categoryConventions: The category splits into two dated looks and one emerging one. Dated look A is 2013-era nonprofit web: CaringBridge and Lotsa Helping Hands — teal/soft-blue, rounded sans, stock photography of smiling multigenerational families on a porch, heavy chrome, small type. Reviewers say it outright: CaringBridge 'feels dated' and 'is behind in terms of current tech'; Lotsa 'needs a massive facelift'. Dated look B is clinical SaaS: dashboards, dense cards, hospital blue, tiny labels, a med-adherence donut chart nobody asked for. Roughly 72% of top healthcare brands use blue as their primary color, so blue reads as generic to the point of invisibility. The 2026 direction that reads current is warm rather than clinical: 'soft colors, warm photography and generous typography', large touch targets, minimal navigation depth, high contrast, reduced motion, and complexity pushed off the primary screen. What specifically reads amateur in 2026: gray placeholder-looking accents, sub-16px body text, hairline dividers, icon-only buttons, and any nursery-pastel or cartoon illustration — a person caring for a dying parent finds cheerfulness patronizing.
aesthetic.emotionalContext: The person writing is exhausted, usually the adult daughter or son, often mid-conflict with a sibling who thinks they are doing too little or too much. 63 million Americans are family caregivers; 78% report burnout, 87% report stress and anxiety, and disrupted sleep is one of the defining symptoms. Entries get written standing in a hallway, in a parked car, in a hospital waiting room with one bar of signal, and at 2am after a fall — often one-handed, often through tears, sometimes by a hired aide whose first language is not English. Two hard consequences for design. First, physical: 17–18px minimum body text, 44–48px minimum tap targets, 7:1 contrast on body copy, no color-only signals, no motion that has to finish before you can type, and a genuinely good dark mode because a large share of entries happen in a dim room at night. Second, tonal: this log is quietly evidence — in sibling disputes, in conversations with doctors, occasionally in guardianship questions — so timestamps and attribution must be unambiguous and permanent-feeling, and the interface must never be jaunty. No confetti, no streaks, no gamification, no 'Great job!' Empty states should be plain and useful, not encouraging. And the app must hold grief without dramatizing it: the log will one day end, and the person will keep it.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: warm, unhurried, dignified, plainspoken, legible-first, quietly sturdy

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: deep muted mulberry / dusk plum — light-mode accent around #7A3B5A (hue ~328, moderate chroma, dark enough for white text at ~7:1), dark-mode accent around #E3A6BE on a warm-dark ground (#1A1216-ish) with #2A1220 ink
colorRecommendation.rationale: Three constraints converge here. (1) Emotional fit: mulberry reads as dusk — warm-leaning, calm, dignified, adult. It is the color of evening lamplight rather than a hospital corridor, which is exactly the register for a family notebook that holds both 'gave the 2pm pill' and 'she didn't know who I was today'. It carries seriousness without gloom and warmth without cheer. (2) In-category distinctiveness: with ~72% of healthcare brands on blue and the two biggest incumbents (CaringBridge, Caring Village) sitting in teal/green, a desaturated plum is effectively unclaimed in caregiving software and will not be mistaken for a hospital portal. (3) Portfolio separation — I audited the repo's 23 apps directly. Occupied territory is violet #7c3aed (baby-log, image-compressor, seating-chart, wedding-timeline), blue #2563eb/#1d4ed8 (bill-splitter, signup-sheets, team-parent, pdf-tools, signature-maker), amber #b45309 (bracket-maker, moving-boxes, sitter-sheet), teal #0f766e (grocery-list, home-inventory, packing-list, scan-to-pdf), forest #2f6b4f (sub-plans), red #b91c1c (secret-santa), hot pink #be185d (wheel-picker), near-black (qr-maker). Caregiver Log is currently on slate #57606d — which it shares with pill-schedule, its single most confusable neighbor. That collision has to be broken. I considered terracotta/clay (#9A4B33) and rejected it: it sits close to the amber trio, and one of those apps is sitter-sheet — 'notes for the person watching my kid' — the app most functionally confusable with a caregiver log, so a hue collision there is the costliest one available. Mulberry's nearest neighbor is wheel-picker's hot pink, but at far lower chroma and lightness, and a random-picker toy is never confused with a care log. Use the accent sparingly — headers, the primary log button, the day marker — on a warm off-white ground (#FBF8F7, not pure white) so long text sessions stay soft.
colorRecommendation.avoid: Clinical blue in any shade: it is the category's own cliché at ~72% adoption and five apps in our portfolio already sit there. Hospital teal and mint green: CaringBridge and Caring Village both live there, so it reads as an imitation of the incumbents users already find dated. The current slate gray #57606d: it reads unfinished and institutional, and it duplicates pill-schedule. Bright pastels, nursery palettes and cartoon illustration: patronizing to an adult caring for a dying parent, and baby-log already owns that emotional register in the portfolio. Red as a primary or accent — reserve it strictly for the 'already given / do not repeat' double-dose warning, per clinical convention (red means genuine urgency), and secret-santa owns red anyway. Also avoid pure black on pure white: at 17-18px in a dim room it glares; use warm-dark and warm-off-white grounds instead.

confidence: Medium-high on competitors and pricing; medium on complaint verbatims. Verified first-hand by fetching the source: Caring Village's full pricing table (Free = 1 village / 2 members / ads shown; Circle $14.99/mo; Village $24.99/mo; ad-free and printable calendar are paid features), Keepsake's 2026 roundup (per-app weaknesses, the iOS/Android fragmentation quote, the 'biggest reason these apps fail' quote), and Neela's comparison table (Neela $12/mo, Medisafe 2-med free cap as of Jan 2026, Caring Village from $14.99). Also verified first-hand: the portfolio color audit, done by grepping --accent tokens across all 23 apps in /workspaces/SWS-apps/apps. LIMITATION on user sentiment — I could not reach primary review sources. WebFetch is blocked for reddit.com and old.reddit.com, and site:reddit.com searches returned App Store listings instead of threads, so I have zero direct Reddit quotes; apps.apple.com review pages returned 404, justuseapp returned 403, and appgrooves.com did not resolve. The 1-3 star complaints (Lotsa's 'cannot edit a misspelled note', 'crashes during login', CaringBridge's 'freezes randomly' / 'does not notify you when someone comments', the $650 Tributes anecdote, the Medisafe 'just greed' reaction) came through aggregator summaries — ComplaintsBoard, marlvel.ai, pillo.care, Trustpilot and search snippets — so treat exact wording as paraphrase-grade rather than quotable verbatim. Specifically unverified: Lotsa Helping Hands' current star rating first-hand (Keepsake says 'mid-2s'); whether Caring Village's free-tier ads are third-party display ads or in-house upsells (their pricing page only lists 'Ad-free experience' as a paid feature, which implies ads but does not describe them); CaringBridge's current visual design, since caringbridge.org returned empty content on fetch — the 'feels dated' judgment is secondhand from Keepsake and reviewer quotes, not my own inspection. Caregiver burnout statistics (63M caregivers, 78% burnout, 87% stress) come from secondary aggregators citing AARP and A Place for Mom's 2025 survey, not the primary reports.
